resources.string: How the adrenal medulla releases hormones

A qualitative view of normal human adrenal medulla function, from sympathetic input to hormone release and return toward resting levels. The adrenal cortex is shown only for orientation. Anatomy, timing, and particle counts are schematic.
Find the medulla inside the gland
An adrenal gland sits above each kidney. In this cutaway of one gland, the outer cortex surrounds the inner medulla, where chromaffin cells are found.
A preganglionic sympathetic nerve carries a signal to the medulla. Its ending releases acetylcholine, which crosses the small gap and activates receptors on a chromaffin cell.
Activation lets calcium enter the chromaffin cell. The rise in calcium helps vesicles fuse with the cell membrane and release stored catecholamines outside the cell.
Epinephrine (adrenaline) and norepinephrine (noradrenaline) enter nearby capillaries. The bloodstream carries these catecholamine hormones beyond the gland.
As sympathetic input eases, the medulla releases less. The body continues to clear circulating catecholamines, so their levels move back toward resting levels rather than falling to zero.

Evidence: circulating catecholamines return toward resting levels in humans
